passage:
The colony water tank had a rusty ladder, and Yogesh was already halfway up. "Come on, Keerthana! Everyone's done it!"
Keerthana, ten, looked at the ladder. The third rung was bent. Her stomach felt tight.
"Chicken!" Yogesh shouted. The others started flapping their arms and clucking.
Her face went hot. If she didn't climb, they might not call her for cricket tomorrow. They might laugh about it at school.
She put one hand on the cold rail. Then she remembered Amma saying the tank was locked for a reason.
"I'll keep score for cricket instead," she said, her voice small.
Some of them kept clucking. Keerthana walked to the bench anyway, heart thumping, and didn't look back.

qa.q: What was bent on the ladder?
qa.a: The third rung was bent.

qa.q: What was Keerthana worried about when they called her chicken?
qa.a: She worried they would not call her for cricket tomorrow and would laugh about it at school.

qa.q: Which choice at the ladder showed good judgement?
qa.a: Remembering Amma's warning and offering to keep score instead kept her safe while still trying to stay part of the group.

qa.q: What would change if one other child had also refused to climb?
qa.a: Keerthana would feel less alone, the clucking might stop, and it would be easier for others to say no too.

grounding: A ten-year-old is called chicken and told everyone has done it to push her up an unsafe ladder, and fear of being left out pulls hard against her judgement.

passage:
"Do it, Gautam. Hide Nikhil's tiffin in the dustbin," Pooja whispered at break. "Everyone did it to new kids last year."
"Why?"
"It's funny! Unless you're scared."
"I'm not scared."
"Then do it." Pooja nudged the steel box towards him. Three others watched from the window, grinning.
Gautam looked at Nikhil, who sat alone reading a comic. "He'll be hungry."
"Oh, so you're his best friend now?" someone called. "Baby Gautam!"
Gautam's ears burned. He wanted them to like him. He had only joined their group in June.
"I'm not doing it," he said, barely audible.
"Fine. Don't sit with us, then."
Gautam picked up his own tiffin and stood there, not sure where to go.

qa.q: What did Pooja dare Gautam to do?
qa.a: Pooja dared Gautam to hide Nikhil's tiffin in the dustbin.

qa.q: Why did Gautam's ears burn?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of losing the group, since he had only joined in June and wanted them to like him.

qa.q: What could help Gautam as he stands there with his tiffin?
qa.a: He could go and sit with Nikhil, who is alone, and later tell a teacher about the dare, so he is not left on his own for saying no.

qa.q: How might Nikhil feel if he learned what almost happened?
qa.a: Nikhil might feel hurt at being a target but grateful that Gautam refused.

grounding: A boy is taunted as scared and a baby to make him hide a new boy's lunch, and fear of being left out weighs against doing right.

passage:
Monday. After school, Varun and three older kids stood by the water-tank ladder in the colony. "Rashmi, climb to the top. Everyone's done it. Or are you chicken?" Rashmi's legs felt wobbly. She said no. They laughed and walked off without her.
Tuesday. At the park, nobody saved her a swing. Varun said, "Only brave people can join our gang." Rashmi sat alone on the bench, fighting tears. She badly wanted to be in the gang again.
Wednesday. They dared her again. She put one foot on the ladder, her heart pounding, then stepped back and ran home.
She told her Mummy everything, crying. Mummy hugged her. "You were brave to say no. That ladder is dangerous." That same evening, Mummy went to the society office. The secretary locked the ladder gate, and Mummy spoke calmly to Varun's parents too.

qa.q: What did the kids dare Rashmi to climb?
qa.a: The water-tank ladder in the colony.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel sitting alone on the bench?
qa.a: Rashmi felt lonely and left out, fighting tears because she badly wanted to belong.

qa.q: What did Rashmi's Mummy do the same evening?
qa.a: She went to the society office, where the secretary locked the ladder gate, and she spoke calmly to Varun's parents.

qa.q: How might Varun see the dare?
qa.a: Varun probably sees it as a test of bravery for the gang, without thinking about the danger or how left out Rashmi feels.

grounding: It shows a child dared and called chicken over several days to climb a dangerous ladder, the fear of exclusion, and an adult acting the same day.

passage:
Asif, you asked why I don't like it when your friends say "everyone does it." Let your Sunaina Nani tell you.
When I was ten, a new girl came to our school. The older girls said, "Hide her tiffin. Everyone's doing it. If you don't, you're not one of us."
I didn't want to. My stomach hurt just thinking of it. But I wanted to belong more than anything. So I hid it behind the water tank.
She searched for it all lunch, crying. The others laughed. I laughed too, and felt sick.
That evening I couldn't eat. I told my mother. She didn't shout. She said, "Tomorrow you find it, give it back, and say sorry. And sit with her." I did.
She became my best friend for forty years, Asif. And those older girls? I can't even remember their names.

qa.q: Where did young Sunaina hide the new girl's tiffin?
qa.a: She hid it behind the water tank.

qa.q: How did young Sunaina feel when she laughed along?
qa.a: She felt sick and guilty, laughing only because she was afraid of not belonging.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed a better choice?
qa.a: Her mother told her to return the tiffin, apologise and sit with the girl, and Sunaina did it the next day.

qa.q: How might the new girl have felt searching for her tiffin?
qa.a: The new girl felt hurt and humiliated, crying while the others laughed.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being pressured with "everyone's doing it" into an unkind act as a child, and how the need to belong outweighed her judgement.

passage:
At the school picnic by the river, the teacher had gone back to the bus for the first-aid box, and the boys had wandered to the railway track.
"Yogesh, cross before the next train," Chaitanya said. "We all did it last year. Or are you a baby?"
The others chanted, "Baby! Baby!" A train horn sounded far away.
Yogesh's knees shook. He wanted to belong so much that he stepped toward the track. Then he pictured his mother's face, and stepped back.
"I'm not doing it," he said, and ran back, face burning.
The teacher was just returning. He told her everything. She walked straight to the track and brought every boy back. Then she called the principal and sat with the group, explaining why nobody would go near the track again.

qa.q: Where had the teacher gone?
qa.a: Back to the bus for the first-aid box.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when the boys chanted "Baby"?
qa.a: Yogesh felt scared and ashamed, so eager to belong that he nearly stepped onto the track.

qa.q: What did the teacher do after Yogesh told her?
qa.a: She walked straight to the track, brought every boy back, called the principal and explained the danger to the whole group.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the dare?
qa.a: Chaitanya probably sees it as a test of courage and belonging, without facing how dangerous it really is.

grounding: It shows a child taunted to join a dangerous dare, the pull of belonging, and an adult acting on the spot when he reports it.

passage: Behind the apartment block in Chennai, Karthik pointed at the water-tank ladder. "Everyone in our gang has touched the top. Unless you're chicken, Pradeep." The others started clucking. Pradeep's face burned. He put one foot on the rusty rung, then another. The ladder wobbled. His stomach flipped. If he came down, they'd laugh all week. If he went up... He came down. "Chicken!" they shouted. At home he couldn't eat his dosa. Amma asked what was wrong, and it all tumbled out. She hugged him. "Coming down was the brave part." Then she called the society secretary, who padlocked the ladder that evening, and she messaged the other parents too.

qa.q: What did Karthik say everyone in the gang had done?
qa.a: Touched the top of the water tank.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel on the ladder?
qa.a: Pradeep felt scared, his stomach flipping, but also afraid of being laughed at all week if he came down.

qa.q: What did Amma do, and why was it important?
qa.a: She praised coming down as brave, then called the society secretary to padlock the ladder and messaged the other parents that same evening, keeping all the children safe.

qa.q: What would change if Pradeep had kept quiet at home?
qa.a: The ladder would still be open and the dare could go on, with Pradeep or another child at risk of a fall.

grounding: Shows a child dared and called chicken to climb an unsafe ladder, torn by fear of exclusion, and an adult's same-day protective step.
